Lastly, the notion of ‘public emergency’ is vague and risks causing multi-
ple interpretation. The definition should be specified to include public health 
emergencies; emergencies resulting from environmental degradation and 
major natural disasters, including those exacerbated by climate change; 
and major man-made disasters, such as major cybersecurity incidents. 
Business-to-business data sharing 
Chapter II lays out obligations for manufacturers of connected products and 
providers of related services to make data generated by the use of products 
or related services accessible to user or to a third party upon request by a 
user.

sector information. Given that some of such data may contain sensitive commercial 
information, be it trade secrets, know-how, or simply undergo a reverse engineering leading to 
disclosure of proprietary information, the Data Act should provide adequate safeguards for the 
protection of such information, as well as remedies in case of breach and/or misuse of data 
shared under the B2G obligations imposed by the proposed Data Act. 
 
Chapter VI.

Where on-device access is technically supported, an explicit requirement 
to make this accessible to third parties of the user’s choice should be included. Only such access 
could technically enable the aspiration for real time, continuous access to the full extent of data 
generated by a connected product. Without such a provision, third party service providers 
would always be kept at a serious structural competitive disadvantage, compared to the 
manufacturer.

Relation between the protected interests in the Data Act proposal 
The Data Act aims to protect, i.a., consumers and small businesses, as well as public authorities 
when dealing with exceptional circumstances demanding data. However, the interests of these 
categories of actors are not necessarily aligned, so that choices are made in the Data Act to protect 
some (often SMEs) to the detriment of the others (potentially consumers and public authorities), see 
for instance Art. 7 and 14(2). However, such a choice is debatable.

5. Suggested amendments for recitals 31 and 34 
Recital 31 prescribes that data generated by the use of a product or related service should 
only be made available to a third party at the request of the user.  This wording seems to 
suggest a prohibition on sharing data generated by connected devices with third parties 
other than on the basis of a request by the user.

on-device data storage or from a remote server to which the data are 
communicated.

The BMW Group supports the ambition to mitigate any gatekeeper effects that 
discriminate individual parties, whilst ensuring technical feasible and proportionate 
implementations. Therefore, we recommend adapting Art. 3.1.:  
Article 3.1.: 
Products shall be designed and manufactured, and related services shall be 
provided, in such a manner that data generated by their use and reasonably 
available to the data holder are, by default, easily, securely and, where relevant 
and appropriate, directly accessible to the user into the same extent as it is 
reasonably available to the data holder. Access can be granted directly from an 
on-device data storage or from a remote server to which the data are 
communicated.

Processing and transferring 
data is technically dependent and limited to existing resources. Thus, providing data 
for exceptional need may cause damages in terms of deprioritizing use cases and 
thereby contractual obligations. On later part, we would recommend amending Article  
2.2.: 
Art. 2.2.:  
Where the data holder claims compensa tion for making data available in 
compliance with a request made pursuant to Article 15, points (b) or (c), such 
compensation shall not exceed damages and the technical and organisational 
costs incurred to comply with the request including, where necessary, the costs of 
anonymisation and of technical adaptation, plus a reasonable margin.
